html:
The family code of Morocco, deeply reformed in 2004 to give women more rights in marriage, divorce and the family.

Morocco's first code after independence, of 1957 and 1958, was drawn from the Maliki school of Islamic law. It made wives owe obedience to their husbands, let men take more than one wife and divorce at will, and required women to have a male guardian to marry. Women's groups campaigned for change for decades, and in 2000 rival marches in Rabat and Casablanca showed how divided the country was.

King Mohammed VI set up a commission and presented the new code as faithful to Islam. Its main changes:

  • the minimum age of marriage rose to 18 for women and men;
  • husband and wife share responsibility for the family;
  • a woman can marry without a guardian;
  • divorce became possible by mutual consent and at the wife's request, with men's repudiation put under court control;
  • a second wife needs a judge's leave and the first wife's knowledge.

Judges still allow many marriages of girls under 18, and a further reform has been debated since 2023. Neighbouring Tunisia had gone further much earlier with its Code of Personal Status of 1956.
sum: The family code of Morocco, deeply reformed in 2004 to give women more rights in marriage, divorce and the family.
